planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 65F; plants run tall, so site where they won't shade shorter crops.

directions: Bred by Campbell Soup Company in 1950 from a cross of several classic okra lines specifically to hold color and texture through canning, still a good choice for anyone processing okra rather than just eating it fresh. Pods stay tender even at 4-5 inches, which forgives missed picking days in a hot Gulf Coast August. It is drought-tolerant once established despite its warm-season water needs during fruit set.

planting.note: Plant slips after soil has warmed above 65F into well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; strong low-spray option where sweetpotato weevil pressure is severe.

directions: Released in 2010 by USDA-ARS Charleston, South Carolina as a very sweet, orange-fleshed, scarlet-skinned cultivar bred specifically for high resistance to soil insects, including sweetpotato weevil, and nematodes, a strong low-spray option for sandy Gulf Coast soils. It bakes with excellent moist, sweet flesh, and bedded roots sprout uniform, transplant-ready slips reliably.
sources: USDA ARS - Notice of release of Charleston Scarlet

planting.note: Plant slips after soil has warmed above 65F into sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; a good nematode-resistant option for sandy Gulf Coast ground where standard boniato varieties struggle.

directions: Developed jointly by USDA-ARS and Clemson University as the first multiple-pest-resistant boniato release, highly resistant to nematodes and moderately resistant to soil insects and Fusarium wilt. Dry, light-yellow flesh with dark-red skin gives a notably bland, starchy character closer to a true potato-eating experience than a dessert-sweet type, and unlike most boniatos it doesn't darken after peeling, which makes it more forgiving for home cooks doing Caribbean or Latin-style preparations.
sources: ScienceDaily - Not-So-Sweet Potato Resists Pests, Disease
